Agree a two-minute review with two questions only: what actually happened, and what would a kind observer say. Then a physical switch. Practice on the last event the client replayed.

fields.label: The event I keep replaying
What I replay most (a sentence, a look, a pause)
My two-minute review: what actually happened
What a kind observer would say
My switch when the two minutes are up
How long the replay used to last, and how long it lasted this time

title: Social Prediction Log
summary: Records the client's forecast before a social situation and the outcome after, to compare over weeks.
goal: Build the client's own evidence that their predictions run far worse than events.
body_md: The forecast must be specific and rated: they will notice me blushing and think less of me, seventy percent. Afterward the client records what observably happened, not how it felt. Review the gap across ten entries, which is usually where belief shifts rather than in any single event.

fields.label: The upcoming situation
What I predict will happen, specifically
How sure I am (0-100%)
What observably happened
How I know (what people said or did)
How the prediction compared
What I predict next time, adjusted

title: Conversation Toolkit Card
summary: A pocket card of openers, follow-up questions and graceful exits for social situations.
goal: Reduce the load of inventing conversation so the client can practice being in it.
body_md: Build it with the client's own words, not scripts from a book, and include exits, since knowing they can leave makes staying easier. Warn against using it as a safety behavior: the card is for learning, and the goal is to need it less. Rehearse a full opener-question-exit in session.

fields.label: Three openers I could actually say
Three follow-up questions that work in most conversations
Two ways to leave a conversation gracefully
What I will do with my hands
The one I will try first this week
How it went, and whether I needed the card

title: Social Brave Steps for Teens
summary: A teen's own ladder of social situations from easy to hard, with a brave step per week.
goal: Give a teenager a graded, self-chosen path back into the social situations they have been dodging.
body_md: Let the teen build and order the steps; a ladder chosen by an adult will not be climbed. Keep parents to a support role agreed on the sheet. Steps should be specific: ask one question in class, not participate more. Celebrate attempts, not outcomes, and expect a step to be repeated before moving up.

fields.label: Situations I have been avoiding
My ladder, easiest at the bottom
This week's step
What I am afraid will happen
What actually happened
What my parent will do (and not do) to help
The step for next week

title: Continuing Bonds Letter
summary: A letter to the person who died, about what has happened since and what the client still carries of them.
goal: Support an ongoing connection with the person rather than a closing of the door.
body_md: Offer it as one option among several, since some clients find writing to the dead unbearable and others find it the only thing that helps. Frame the bond as something that changes rather than ends. The client decides whether to read it aloud, keep it, or take it somewhere. Include 988 among the prompts for the darkest hours.

fields.label: What I want to tell you about since you died
What I have kept of you (a habit, a phrase, an object, a way of seeing)
What I wish I had said
What I think you would say to me now
How I will keep you in my life going forward
If the grief ever gets dangerously dark: 988 (call or text), and who else I will reach

title: Grief Triggers Calendar
summary: A year at a glance with the dates, seasons and events likely to bring the grief up hard.
goal: Let the client see the hard days coming and plan support for them instead of being ambushed.
body_md: Include the obvious dates and the sideways ones: the first snow, the tax season the person used to handle, the song at the store. Plan for the week before an anniversary, which is often worse than the day. Decide with the client who will know about each date.

fields.label: Anniversaries and birthdays
Seasons, holidays and rituals that will be different
Sideways reminders I can predict
The next hard date, and what I will do that day
Who will know it is coming
What helped on the last hard date, and what did not

title: Dual Process Week Planner
summary: A week planned with time for facing the loss and time for the ordinary business of living, both on purpose.
goal: Normalize moving between grief and daily life instead of feeling guilty about either.
body_md: Explain that healthy grief moves between the loss and the rest of life, and that neither side is avoidance. Clients stuck on one side feel guilty when they laugh, or numb when they cannot cry; the planner gives both permission. Keep the entries small and concrete.

fields.label: Times this week I will let myself be with the loss (looking at photos, visiting, talking about them)
Times this week I will do ordinary or even pleasant things
The side I tend to get stuck on
What guilt says when I switch sides
What I will say back to it
How the week went

title: Memory Box Project
summary: A child decorates a box and fills it with objects, drawings and stories that hold the person who died.
goal: Give a grieving child a concrete, permitted place for their memories and a way to talk about them.
body_md: Let the child lead on what goes in and what stays private. Each item comes with a story the child tells if they want to; the telling is the work. Involve the surviving parent or carer where possible, and coach them to follow the child's pace rather than their own. Revisit the box on hard dates.

fields.label: What my box looks like
The first three things I put in it, and why
A story that goes with one of them
Something I want to ask about the person who died
Who I can open the box with
When I might want to open it

title: Grief Conversation Cards
summary: A deck of gentle prompts about the person who died, drawn in turn by family members or a group.
goal: Let a family or group talk about the person in a structured, low-pressure way.
body_md: Write the prompts with the group first so nothing on a card ambushes anyone, mixing light ones with heavier ones. Any card can be passed. Play in a circle with a talking object. In families, children often answer more freely than adults, which gives the adults permission.

fields.label: Prompts we put on the cards
The card I drew, and what I said
Something I learned about the person from someone else
A card I passed on
The card I would like to answer next time

title: Needs Inventory for Partners
summary: Each partner lists their needs in the relationship, ranked, and guesses their partner's list before comparing.
goal: Replace assumed needs with stated ones, and show each partner what the other has been guessing.
body_md: Have both partners complete it separately, including the guess about each other, before any discussion. The gaps between the guess and the real list are the material. Keep the tone of curiosity when a partner's need surprises the other; surprise is information, not an accusation.

fields.label: My top five needs in this relationship, ranked
How well each is being met right now (0-10)
What I think my partner's top five are
What surprised me about their real list
One need of theirs I could meet better this month
One need of mine I will ask for directly

title: Perpetual Problems Sorter
summary: Sorts a couple's recurring arguments into the solvable and the perpetual, and plans a different approach to each.
goal: Stop a couple from trying to solve what needs managing, and from managing what could be solved.
body_md: List the arguments first, then sort. Perpetual problems come from differences in personality or values and will be there in ten years; the goal is dialogue and humor about them, not a fix. Solvable problems get a concrete plan. Most couples are relieved to hear that having perpetual problems is normal.

fields.label: Arguments we have more than once a month
Which of these come from a difference in who we are
Which could actually be solved with a plan
For one solvable problem: our plan
For one perpetual problem: what we can each accept
How we will talk about the perpetual one next time it comes up

title: Trust Rebuilding Steps
summary: A shared ladder of specific, observable actions that would rebuild trust after a breach, with a timeline.
goal: Turn a vague demand to earn trust back into steps both partners can see happening.
body_md: The hurt partner names what would help; the other partner says what they can commit to. Steps must be observable, since promises to change are not. Agree how long the checking phase lasts, because trust cannot rebuild under permanent surveillance. Review progress monthly in session.

fields.label: What was broken, in one sentence each
Actions that would help me trust again (specific and visible)
Which of these I can commit to, and when
What transparency looks like for now, and for how long
What I need to hear when I have a wobble
How we will mark progress

title: Communication Pattern Replay
summary: Replays one recent exchange line by line, with each partner naming what they meant and what they heard.
goal: Show a couple the gap between what was said, what was meant and what landed.
body_md: Pick a short exchange, not the biggest fight. Write the actual lines, then have each partner add what they meant and what they heard. The gaps are usually where the fight lives. Finish by rewriting two lines each, and rehearse the rewrite in session.

fields.label: The exchange, line by line, as it happened
For my lines: what I meant
For their lines: what I heard
Where the gap between meant and heard was widest
Two lines I would rewrite
How the rewritten version sounds out loud

title: Relationship Values Compass
summary: Each partner names the kind of partner they want to be, separately from how the other is behaving.
goal: Anchor each partner to their own values so change does not wait on the other person moving first.
body_md: Works with a couple or with one partner alone. The key move is separating my values as a partner from what I get back; clients often discover they have been acting on a scoreboard. Choose one valued action for the week that does not depend on the other person's response.

fields.label: The partner I want to be, in three words
How I have actually been acting lately
What I have been waiting for my partner to do first
One valued action I will take this week regardless
What my mind says will happen if I go first
What actually happened

title: Safety and Stabilization Plan
summary: A plan for the practical and emotional safety a survivor needs in place before any deeper work.
goal: Put steady ground under the client first: who, where, what, and what to do when it gets too much.
body_md: Complete it together in session and never as homework. Cover present-day safety from the person who harmed them, the people who help, the skills that bring them back, and what to do in the worst hours. Move at the client's pace and do not ask for the details of what happened; that is not what this sheet is for. Include 988.

fields.label: Am I safe from the person now? What would make me safer
People I trust, and what each one can help with
Skills that bring me back when I am flooded
Signs that I am doing too much too fast
What I will do in the worst hour: 988 (call or text), and my other numbers
What I want my therapist to know about pace
What I am not ready to talk about yet, and that is fine

title: Consent and Boundaries Map
summary: Maps the client's yes, no and maybe across touch, closeness and conversation, in their own words.
goal: Help a survivor reclaim the right to decide, in small everyday ways, what they allow and what they do not.
body_md: Keep it to everyday boundaries at first: hugs, sitting close, questions from family, who has their number. The maybe column matters, since survivors often feel boundaries must be absolute to count. Rehearse one no in session. Nothing here asks about the abuse itself.

fields.label: Things I am a clear yes to
Things I am a clear no to
Things that are a maybe, and what would make them a yes
A boundary someone in my life keeps crossing
How I will say no to that, in my words
What I will do if they push
Someone who respects my boundaries well

title: Shame Response Sheet
summary: Catches the self-blame that follows abuse, tests it against what the client would say to another survivor, and writes the fairer version.
goal: Loosen the belief that the client caused, allowed or deserved what happened.
body_md: Do this in session, gently, and expect the double standard to be stark: the client will extend to another survivor a compassion they refuse themselves. Do not argue the client out of the belief; let the comparison do the work, and rate belief before and after. Stop if the client becomes flooded and return to grounding.

fields.label: What I tell myself about why it happened
How much I believe that (0-100%)
What I would say to a friend who told me the same story
Where the blame actually belongs
The fairer statement, in my words
How much I believe the fairer statement now (0-100%)

title: Support Disclosure Planner
summary: Plans whether, who, when and how much to tell, so a disclosure happens on the client's terms.
goal: Keep the choice of who knows, and how much, in the survivor's hands.
body_md: Not telling is a valid outcome of this sheet and should be said out loud. Work through what the client wants from telling, who is likely to respond well, and how much to say; a first sentence and an exit line are worth rehearsing. Plan for the reaction being disappointing, since it sometimes is.

fields.label: What I hope telling someone would give me
People I might tell, and how I think each would respond
The person I would tell first, if anyone
How much I want to say (a sentence is enough)
My first sentence
How I will end the conversation if I need to
What I will do for myself afterward, whatever their reaction

title: Body Safety Rules Poster
summary: A child makes a poster of body safety rules: private parts, okay and not-okay touch, secrets versus surprises, and who to tell.
goal: Teach a child the words and the permission to tell, as part of prevention work with families.
body_md: A prevention and education tool, done with a parent in the room where possible. Use correct names for body parts. Teach that surprises are fun and short and secrets about bodies are never kept. List five trusted adults. If a child discloses during this, stop the activity, stay calm, believe them, and follow your mandated reporting duties.

fields.label: Private parts have proper names, and mine are
Okay touch and not-okay touch: my examples
The difference between a surprise and a secret
My five trusted grown-ups
What I say if someone breaks a body safety rule
Where my poster will hang

title: Coping Menu by Situation
summary: A menu of the client's coping options sorted by where they are: at work, in public, at home, in bed.
goal: Match skills to settings so the right one is available where the distress actually happens.
body_md: Most clients have skills that only work at home and distress that happens elsewhere. Sort by setting and check that each setting has at least two options that are invisible to other people. Include one for the middle of the night. Keep the menu in the phone's notes.

fields.label: At work or school: two things I can do without anyone noticing
In public: two options
At home: two options
In bed at 3 a.m.: two options
The skill I reach for too often, and where it does not work
The new skill I will try this week, and where

title: Skill Practice Log
summary: A weekly log of which coping skill the client used, in what situation, and how well it worked.
goal: Turn coping from a vague resolve into a tracked practice with results.
body_md: The rating is the useful part: a skill that scores three out of ten in three different situations can be retired without guilt. Look for the mismatch between skills tried and situations faced. Praise the attempt, especially when the skill did not work, since trying is what builds the habit.

fields.label: Date and the situation
Distress before (0-10)
The skill I used
Distress after (0-10)
How well it worked (0-10) and why
A skill I could have used instead
The skill I will practice most next week

title: Coping Ladder for Kids
summary: A ladder of a child's coping moves from small feelings at the bottom to big ones at the top.
goal: Match the size of the coping move to the size of the feeling, in a picture a child can use.
body_md: Draw a ladder with three or four rungs and let the child assign feelings sizes to each. Small feelings get small moves: a breath, a drink of water. Big feelings get big moves: a break, a grown-up. Practice one move per rung in session and have the parent post the ladder at home.

fields.label: Bottom rung: a small feeling and my small move
Middle rung: a medium feeling and my medium move
Top rung: a huge feeling and my biggest move
How I know which rung I am on
Who helps me on the top rung
Where my ladder is posted

title: Coping Skills Relay
summary: Teams race to act out or demonstrate a coping skill for each situation card drawn.
goal: Rehearse coping skills under mild pressure and laughter, so they are practiced rather than just known.
body_md: Write situation cards with the group beforehand: a test tomorrow, a friend ignoring a text, a loud house. A team scores when the skill fits the situation and could actually be done there. Judge fit, not speed, and let the group argue the call; the argument is the learning.

fields.label: Situation cards we made
Skills my team demonstrated
A skill another team showed that I want to steal
A situation none of us could match well
The skill I will practice this week

title: Helpful vs Costly Coping Sort
summary: Sorts everything the client does to feel better into what helps in the long run and what costs more than it gives.
goal: Help the client judge coping by its long-term workability rather than by how fast it works.
body_md: List everything without judgment first, including the ones the client is ashamed of; those are usually the fastest-acting. Sort by long-term workability, not by how they look. Most clients find a few things belong in both columns depending on amount, which is worth writing down rather than resolving.

fields.label: Everything I do to feel better, fast or slow
Which ones help me next week too
Which ones cost more than they give
Which ones depend on how much
One costly one I will shrink, and how
One helpful one I will do more of, and when

title: Phobia Prediction Tracker
summary: Records what the client expects to happen around the feared object or situation and what actually occurs.
goal: Build the client's own evidence that the feared outcome and the felt danger diverge.
body_md: Ask for the specific feared outcome, not just fear: I will faint, the dog will bite, the plane will crash. Rate belief before and after each approach. The pattern across entries is what changes belief, so aim for at least eight entries before drawing conclusions together.

fields.label: The feared thing and the situation
What I predict will happen, specifically
How sure I am (0-100%)
Peak fear (0-10)
What actually happened
What I did during the peak
My belief in the prediction now (0-100%)

title: Approach Steps Planner
summary: Plans the next approach step toward a feared object in detail: where, how long, with whom, and what to drop.
goal: Make each approach step concrete enough to actually happen this week.
body_md: One step at a time, planned to the minute. Include what safety moves the client will drop, since carrying the escape plan into the step blunts it. Decide in advance how long to stay: long enough for the fear to fall, not just to touch and run. Debrief in session before planning the next.

fields.label: This week's step
Where and when, exactly
Who will be there, and what they will and will not do
How long I will stay (until fear drops by half)
The safety moves I will not use
What happened, and what I will do next week

title: Phobia Body Response Sheet
summary: Names what the client's body does around the feared thing, and separates the alarm from the danger.
goal: Help the client see the fear response as an alarm that can fire without a fire.
body_md: Map the response: heart, breath, muscles, stomach, the urge to run. Explain plainly that the body's alarm is doing its job and that the job is to get them out, which is why staying feels wrong. For blood or needle fears, note the faint response and plan applied tension separately.

fields.label: What my body does first around the feared thing
What it does next
The urge that comes with it
What the alarm is trying to make me do
What I know about the real danger in this situation
What I will do with the alarm next time it fires

title: Brave Practice Chart for Kids
summary: A sticker chart for a child's repeated brave practices with a feared thing, tied to a small reward.
goal: Make repetition of approach steps visible and rewarding for a child.
duration: 20 minutes to set up, then daily
body_md: Choose practices small enough to repeat daily: look at a picture of a dog, stand in the doorway with the lights off. Stickers go on for attempts, not for calm. Parents hold the chart and the reward and keep their own anxiety out of the practice. Change the practice when it stops earning fear.

fields.label: My brave practice this week
Stickers I earned
How scared I was the first time (0-10) and the last time
My reward when the chart is full
What my grown-up does during practice
Next week's brave practice

title: Fear Ladder Card Sort
summary: Situations written on cards and physically sorted into a ladder from least to most scary.
goal: Build a fear hierarchy as a hands-on sorting task rather than a form.
body_md: Write one situation per card with the client, at least fifteen, then sort them on the table or floor. The physical sorting draws out distinctions a form misses, and the client can move cards as beliefs change. Photograph the finished ladder and use it to choose the next approach step.

fields.label: Situations we wrote on cards
The bottom three cards
The top three cards
Cards I moved while sorting, and why
The card I will start with
The card I cannot imagine reaching yet

title: Body Neutrality Practice
summary: Daily short statements about what the body did today rather than how it looked.
goal: Move the client's relationship with their body from judgment toward function and use.
duration: Two minutes daily for two weeks
body_md: Aim for neutral, not positive; clients who cannot believe their body is beautiful can believe it carried them up the stairs. Keep the statements about doing and feeling. Notice when the client sneaks an appearance comment in and gently redirect. Never mention weight, shape or food in this practice.

fields.label: Three things my body did for me today
One thing it let me feel (warmth, music, a hug, the wind)
A neutral statement about my body, without judgment either way
What my mind wanted to add about how it looks
How I responded to that
The statement I will use tomorrow morning

title: Body Checking Log
summary: Records the mirror checks, pinching, comparing and photo scrutiny that keep body worry alive, and what each one did to mood.
goal: Show the client how checking feeds the worry, and plan a reduction.
body_md: Checking feels like getting information but produces worse mood almost every time; the log makes that visible. Include the quiet forms: reflections in windows, comparing in group photos, clothes tried and discarded. Plan one check to cut in half, not to stop entirely.

fields.label: Date and time
What I checked, and how (mirror, pinch, photo, comparing)
What I was looking for
Mood before and after (0-10)
How long the reassurance lasted, if any
The check I will cut in half next week
What I will do instead in that moment

title: Appearance Assumptions Sheet
summary: Lists the client's rules linking appearance to worth, acceptance or success, and tests each one.
goal: Loosen the beliefs that make appearance carry the whole weight of self-worth.
body_md: Draw out the if-then rules: if I looked different, then people would... Test each against the client's own experience and the people they admire. The goal is to shrink the share of self-worth that appearance holds, which a pie chart of what makes up their worth can show before and after.

fields.label: My rules about appearance (if I looked..., then...)
Where each rule came from
Evidence from my own life for and against it
People I admire, and how much their looks have to do with it
How much of my self-worth appearance holds now (%)
What else I would like it to rest on

title: Body Gratitude Function List
summary: A list of what the client's body has carried them through, by life stage, written as a record rather than a rating.
goal: Build a history of the body as a companion rather than an object under review.
body_md: Move through life stages: childhood play, illness survived, work done, people carried, places reached. The tone is a record, not a pep talk. Clients with a history of harming or overworking their body may find this tender; slow down there. No comments on shape or size anywhere on the sheet.

fields.label: What my body did for me as a child
What it has carried me through
What it lets me do that I would miss
Someone it has held or helped
Something it recovered from
What I would like to thank it for, plainly

title: Media Diet Audit
summary: An inventory of the accounts, shows and images the client consumes, and what each does to how they feel in their body.
goal: Change what the client feeds their body image, since much of it arrives through a screen.
body_md: Go through the phone together. For each account or habit, ask what it does to the client's body feeling in the ten minutes after. Unfollowing is a real intervention and often the fastest one; replace, do not just remove, so the feed is not empty. Repeat in a month.

fields.label: Accounts and shows I see most
How I feel in my body after each (better, worse, nothing)
The ones that leave me comparing
Accounts I will unfollow or mute this week
What I will follow instead (bodies doing things, other interests entirely)
How my feed feels after the change

title: Double Standard Technique Sheet
summary: Sets the standard a client applies to themselves next to the one they'd offer a friend.
goal: Use it to soften harsh self-judgment by testing it against a kinder standard already in use.
body_md: Ask the client to describe a recent situation where they judged themselves harshly, then to imagine a friend in the identical situation and write out what they'd actually say to that friend. The gap between the two columns is the point — most clients apply a standard to themselves they'd never accept as fair for anyone else, and naming that gap out loud does more than any argument about the thought's accuracy.

fields.label: The situation I judged myself harshly for
What I said to myself about it
A friend in the exact same situation
What I would actually say to that friend
One sentence closer to fair I can say to myself

title: Structured Problem-Solving Worksheet
summary: Walks a client through defining a problem, generating options, and picking one to try.
goal: Use it to replace circular worrying about a problem with a concrete, testable next step.
body_md: This works best on a problem the client has been turning over without acting on, not a crisis needing an immediate decision. The brainstorming step should stay judgment-free — write down every option including bad ones — since clients who edit as they go tend to land back on the option they already rejected. Set a date to review what happened with the option they picked.

fields.label: The problem, stated in one specific sentence
Every option I can think of, including bad ones
Pros and cons of my top two options
The option I will try
My first concrete step
Date I will review how it went

title: Habit Reversal Planner
summary: Pairs an unwanted habit with an early warning sign and a competing response to use instead.
goal: Use it to interrupt an automatic habit at the moment it usually starts, not after.
body_md: Start with awareness before change: have the client track the habit for a few days first so the early warning sign is specific rather than guessed at. The competing response should be something physically incompatible with the habit and easy to do without planning, since anything that requires setup will get skipped in the moment it's actually needed.

fields.label: The habit I want to change
What usually happens right before it (place, feeling, time)
My earliest warning sign that it's about to happen
A competing response I can do instead
Who I've told about this plan
How this week went

title: Procrastination Value Timeline
summary: Compares how good delay feels right now against the cost the client expects later.
goal: Use it to make the short-term relief of putting something off visible against its real cost.
body_md: Clients rarely lack the reasoning to see that delay has a cost — the problem is that the reasoning arrives too late, after the relief of avoiding the task has already been felt. Filling this out ahead of a task the client is likely to delay again gives them something concrete to reread at the moment they reach for the delay instead.

fields.label: The task I keep delaying
How doing it now would feel in the next ten minutes
How delaying it will feel in the next ten minutes
What delaying it will cost me by this time next week
The smallest first step I could take right now

title: Should Statement Rewrite Sheet
summary: Catches a client's rigid should statements and rewrites them as a preference instead.
goal: Use it to loosen the guilt and pressure that rigid should statements tend to create.
body_md: Collect a handful of the client's own should statements before the session rather than inventing examples, since the rewrite lands better on language they actually use. Walk through why the rigid version generates guilt or resentment even when the underlying goal is reasonable, then rewrite it as something the client wants rather than something they're required to do.

fields.label: A should statement I say to myself often
Where I think this rule came from
What it costs me to hold it this rigidly
A rewrite as a preference instead of a rule
How it felt to say the rewrite out loud

title: Silly Voice Defusion Practice
summary: Has a client say a sticky thought aloud in a silly voice to loosen its grip.
goal: Use it to shift a client's relationship to a thought without arguing over whether it's true.
body_md: Pick a thought the client already knows isn't fully accurate but that still pulls at them, then have them say it in a cartoon voice, a slow-motion voice, and their own voice back to back. Some clients laugh, some feel silly and resist — both are useful to discuss. The point isn't to make the thought funny forever, just to prove in the room that its grip can loosen without the content changing at all.

fields.label: The thought that keeps pulling at me
How it felt to hear it in a silly voice
How much it felt like 'the truth' before, out of ten
How much it felt like 'the truth' just after, out of ten
When I could try this again this week

title: Ten-Year Values Letter
summary: Has a client write a letter from ten years ahead describing a life built on their values.
goal: Use it to clarify what actually matters to a client beneath their current worries.
body_md: Ask the client to write as their future self, ten years on, describing an ordinary week lived in line with what matters most to them — not a fantasy of achievement, just the texture of the days. Clients who struggle often default to describing outcomes, a job title, a relationship status, rather than qualities of how they show up; gently redirect toward the latter, since that's what committed action can actually be built from.

fields.label: An ordinary day, ten years from now, if I'm living by what matters to me
What kind of person am I being in that day
What's one thing from that day I could bring into this week
What gets in the way of that right now

title: Sky Mind Observing Practice
summary: Uses the sky and passing weather as a metaphor for the self that notices thoughts and feelings.
goal: Use it to build a client's sense of a stable self that is not the same as their passing thoughts.
body_md: Guide the client to picture themselves as the sky, with each thought, mood, or urge as weather passing through — sometimes calm, sometimes a storm, but the sky itself unchanged underneath. This tends to click for clients who feel defined by whatever mood is loudest that day. Bring it back to a recent difficult moment and ask what stayed constant while the weather in it was rough.

fields.label: A recent difficult moment and what the 'weather' was
What stayed the same underneath that weather
A thought I've been treating as permanent that might just be passing
What I notice trying this practice

title: Willingness Ladder
summary: Ranks situations by how willing a client is to feel discomfort while still moving toward what matters.
goal: Use it to build willingness gradually rather than asking for it all at once.
body_md: Unlike a hierarchy built around reducing distress, this ladder is ranked by willingness — how much discomfort the client is prepared to carry while still taking a values-aligned step. Start low enough that the first rung feels genuinely doable this week, and debrief every attempt by asking what the client did while feeling the discomfort, not whether the discomfort went away.

fields.label: The value this ladder is in service of
A step I'm willing to take even with some discomfort (lowest rung)
A step further up the ladder
The top rung, whether or not I'm ready for it yet
What I noticed after trying the lowest rung

title: Committed Action Contract
summary: A short written agreement a client makes with themselves to take one values-aligned action.
goal: Use it to turn a values discussion into a specific, dated commitment the client can keep or revisit.
body_md: Keep the action small enough to actually happen this week and tie it explicitly back to a value named earlier in the session, not to an outcome the client can't control. When a client doesn't follow through, treat the contract as information about the size of the step rather than a failure, and rewrite it smaller together before ending the session.

fields.label: The value behind this action
The specific action I'm committing to
By when
What might get in the way
How I'll handle that if it happens
My signature and today's date

title: Nonjudgmental Stance Practice
summary: Has a client rewrite a judgmental thought about themselves or others as a plain description.
goal: Use it to build the habit of describing events without automatically evaluating them.
body_md: Judgments tend to escalate emotion by adding a verdict on top of a fact, so this practice asks the client to catch a judgment and translate it into what actually happened, with no good, bad, should, or shouldn't attached. This is harder than it sounds and clients often need a few tries per sentence — that struggle is the skill being built, not a sign it isn't working.

fields.label: A judgmental thought I had recently, exactly as I thought it
The plain facts underneath it, with no verdict attached
How my body felt saying the judgment
How my body felt saying the plain description

title: What Skills Practice Card
summary: Walks a client through observing, describing, then participating in a moment as it happens.
goal: Use it to practice the DBT 'what' skills as a sequence, not just as ideas.
body_md: Have the client pause during an ordinary moment — a meal, a walk, a conversation — and move through the three skills in order: notice what's here without words, then put words to it, then step fully into doing it. Most clients skip straight to participating out of habit, so the card works best used in short, deliberate bursts rather than as a running commentary on the whole day.

fields.label: The moment I practiced with
What I observed, before I put words to it
How I described it
What it was like to then just participate

title: Mastery Moment Planner
summary: Schedules one activity a client can do well as a planned confidence and mood boost.
goal: Use it to build a client's sense of competence on purpose, ahead of a hard stretch.
body_md: The activity needs to be slightly challenging but realistically achievable this week — too easy and it does nothing for confidence, too hard and a client already running low on mood will avoid it. Schedule it like an appointment rather than leaving it to motivation, and check afterward what doing it well actually felt like in the body, not just whether it got done.

fields.label: An activity I can reliably do well, even if small
When this week I'll do it
What might get in the way
How it felt afterward

title: Turning Toward Acceptance Log
summary: Logs the repeated choice to turn toward acceptance of something a client cannot change.
goal: Use it to show a client that acceptance is a decision made again and again, not one event.
body_md: Turning the mind is not the same as being at peace with something — it's the moment of choosing, again, to stop fighting a fact that won't change right now. Clients often expect one big turn to be enough and get discouraged when the resistance comes back an hour later; this log makes the repetition visible and normal instead of a sign the skill isn't working.

fields.label: The fact I keep resisting
A moment today I turned my mind toward accepting it
What pulled me back toward fighting it
How many times I noticed myself turning today

title: Mindfulness of Current Emotion Practice
summary: Has a client observe a strong emotion moving through them without pushing it away or feeding it.
goal: Use it to build tolerance for a feeling's rise and fall without acting on it right away.
body_md: Ask the client to notice where the emotion sits in the body, name it, and watch it rise and change without trying to fix, judge, or extend it — much like watching a wave rather than surfing or fighting it. This is best introduced with a moderate emotion first, not the client's most intense one, so they can build the skill before testing it under real pressure.

fields.label: The emotion I practiced with
Where I felt it in my body
What I noticed as it changed
Whether I acted on it or just watched it

title: Partner Boundary Negotiation Sheet
summary: Has each partner name a boundary they need and negotiate one both can actually keep.
goal: Use it to turn a vague complaint about overstepping into a specific, agreed boundary.
body_md: Have each partner fill out their side alone first, since boundaries proposed in the moment tend to be reactions to the last conflict rather than what's actually needed. In session, look for the version each partner can actually sustain, not the most generous-sounding one — a boundary that gets broken in a week does more damage than a smaller one that holds.

fields.label: Partner A: a boundary I need right now

goal: Use it to make a couple's disagreement about a decision specific instead of circular.
body_md: Works best for a decision with a real deadline — a move, a schedule change, a purchase — rather than an open-ended values debate. Each partner rates every option alone first so the ratings aren't shaped by the other's reaction in the room, then compare where they land closest together and where the real gap is, which is usually smaller than the argument made it feel.

goal: Use it to surface mismatched expectations about a transition before they turn into conflict.
body_md: Any major shared change — a move, a career switch, an aging parent moving in, an empty nest — carries a private list of hopes and losses each partner may not have said out loud. Have both fill this in separately, then read each other's answers before discussing; the gap between what one partner assumed the other felt and what they actually wrote is usually where the real conversation starts.

goal: Use it to build a couple's habit of noticing and reinforcing each other's strengths.
body_md: This is a short, structured exchange, not a general compliment session — each partner names one specific thing they did recently that they're quietly proud of, and the other partner reflects it back in their own words before adding anything of their own. Couples under strain often stop noticing each other's wins at all, and this rebuilds that muscle in a low-stakes, repeatable way.

goal: Use it to replace well-meant nagging with support the changing partner actually asked for.
body_md: The partner making the change should write the first two fields alone, since support that hasn't been requested tends to land as pressure no matter how well intended. Be specific about what to say and when — 'remind me' and 'don't remind me' both need exact wording, or the couple will fall back into the same pattern within a week.

goal: Use it to make abstract friendship skills concrete and easy for a child to picture and reuse.
body_md: Give the child a blank recipe card and ask what 'ingredients' go into being a good friend — sharing, listening, saying sorry — and let them decorate it however they like. Younger children often name actions rather than qualities, which is fine and actually more usable. goal: Use it to give a child a concrete object to picture when a hard moment calls for confidence.
body_md: Cut a simple cape shape from paper and have the child decorate it with drawings or words for things they've done that took courage or skill, however small. Keep the caregiver in the room to help remember real moments the child might not think to name themselves. goal: Use it to make daily habit follow-through visible and rewarding for a child.

goal: Use it to give a child a fun, physical way to pick a coping choice instead of freezing or arguing.
body_md: Have the child draw and decorate several choices around a paper circle — a drink of water, ten jumping jacks, squeezing a pillow, asking for a hug — then attach a spinnable arrow with a brass fastener. The caregiver keeps the wheel somewhere accessible and offers a spin as a first step at the very start of a hard moment, before things escalate, rather than as a punishment afterward.

goal: Use it to teach a child turn-taking and listening through a hands-on family routine.
body_md: Any sturdy stick, spoon, or tube works as the base — the decorating is what makes it the child's. Explain the one rule: whoever holds it talks, everyone else listens, then it passes on. Coach the caregiver to run a short weekly family meeting where each person gets a turn with the stick to share one good thing and one thing they'd like to change, keeping it brief enough that younger children stay engaged.

title: Values Charades
summary: Players act out a value word without speaking while the group guesses which one it is.
goal: Use it to make abstract values concrete and get a group talking about why each one matters.
body_md: Write values like honesty, courage, or connection on separate cards and have players draw one at a time to act out silently while the group guesses. Once a value is guessed, spend a minute asking who in the group already lives that value in some way and how. The guessing is just the warm-up; the debrief about real examples is where the game earns its place in session.

title: Assertive Comeback Relay
summary: Teams race to respond assertively to scripted pushy lines, scoring points for tone as well as words.
goal: Use it to rehearse assertive responses under mild pressure before they're needed for real.
body_md: Prepare a stack of pushy or guilt-tripping lines a player might hear from a friend, boss, or family member. One player reads a line, the next in line has ten seconds to respond assertively — not aggressively, not passively — before the group scores it and the relay moves on. The time pressure is deliberate: real pushback rarely comes with time to plan the perfect line.

goal: Use it to make weekly habit follow-through visible and a little competitive within a group.
duration: 10 minutes at the start of each session
body_md: Draw a simple path board with a few bonus and setback spaces scattered along it. Each player names one habit at the start of the week and moves their token forward one space per day it happened, landing on bonus or setback spaces at random. The debrief matters more than the race: ask what helped on the days a player moved forward and what happened on the days they didn't.

title: The Decision Dice Game
summary: A die with six decision-making steps that players roll before working through a real choice.
goal: Use it to give a group a repeatable structure for talking through a decision out loud.
body_md: Label the six sides of a blank die with steps such as pros, cons, values check, gut check, ask someone, sleep on it. A player names a real decision they're facing, then rolls the die and works through whatever step comes up before rolling again. Rolling the steps out of the usual order tends to surface angles a straight list would have skipped.

title: Friendship Skills Scavenger Hunt

goal: Use it to turn friendship skills into small, trackable actions instead of vague advice.
body_md: Give each player the same short list of friendship actions to look for chances to do that week — compliment someone, invite someone to join in, check in with someone having a hard day. At the next session, go around and have each player report which ones they managed and how it went, treating a missed item as information about what's hard rather than a failure to note.

title: Five-Minute Start Rule Tracker
summary: Tracks whether committing to just five minutes on a delayed task actually got it started.
goal: Use it to test whether lowering the bar to start is enough to break a pattern of delay.
body_md: The rule is simple: commit to five minutes only, with full permission to stop after that. Most of the value here is in the data, not the rule itself — some clients find they keep going past five minutes almost every time, others find they genuinely stop, and that's useful too, since it means the task itself needs breaking down further, not just an easier entry point.

goal: Use it to make an overloaded week visible before it turns into burnout.
body_md: Have the client rate the past week, not an ideal week, across a handful of life domains, then circle the one that got the least attention and wasn't supposed to. This works well as a recurring check-in rather than a one-time exercise, since the pattern across several weeks usually says more than any single week does on its own.

title: Compassionate Pause Card
summary: A short three-step script a client can use in the moment when they're being hard on themselves.
goal: Use it to give a client a fast, repeatable alternative to self-criticism in a difficult moment.
body_md: The three steps are short on purpose so a client can actually use them mid-moment rather than only later in reflection: naming that this is a hard moment, remembering that struggling is something everyone goes through, and offering themselves a kind phrase they choose ahead of time. Have the client write their own phrase in session, since a phrase supplied by someone else rarely feels believable when it's needed.

goal: Use it to build gratitude through one detailed act rather than a running list.
body_md: Unlike a running gratitude list, this asks for one specific person and one specific reason, written as an actual letter. Encourage detail over generality — what they did, when, and how it affected the client specifically — since vague thanks tends to feel flat to write and to read. Whether the client ever sends it is optional; the writing itself is where most of the benefit shows up.

title: Decision Fatigue Reset Plan
summary: Identifies small daily decisions a client can automate or eliminate to save energy for bigger ones.
goal: Use it to free up a client's decision-making energy for the choices that actually matter to them.
body_md: Have the client list the small decisions that repeat every day — what to wear, what to eat, when to check messages — and sort them into ones worth automating (same choice every time) versus ones worth eliminating outright. This tends to land well with clients who describe feeling drained by the end of an ordinary day with no single obvious cause; the fatigue is often the sum of many small, unnecessary decisions rather than one big one.

title: Hyperarousal Interpretation Record
summary: A thought record that reframes a racing heart or jumpiness as an old alarm, not present danger.
goal: Use it to help clients separate a body's alarm response from an actual present-moment threat.
body_md: Run this once grounding skills are already in place, since it asks a client to look closely at body sensations that can themselves feel activating. The work is reinterpretation, not exposure: a sensation gets relabeled as a leftover signal from the body's protective system rather than evidence of current danger. Keep the focus on right now, never on what happened, and pause if a client's arousal climbs instead of settling.

goal: Use it to help clients move from a flooded moment back into one small, values-aligned step.
body_md: Use this right after a spike in distress has already started to ease, not during the worst of it. The two moves matter in order: ground first, then choose, since asking a flooded client to act on values before they are anchored usually fails. Coach clients toward genuinely small actions, since an ambitious choice can undo the settling that grounding just produced.

title: Flashback Recovery Roles Plan
summary: A plan both partners complete for what helps right after a flashback or dissociative moment.
goal: Use it to give partners a rehearsed, agreed script instead of improvising in a hard moment.
body_md: Complete this together while both partners are calm and settled, then revisit it after any real moment to fine-tune it. Keep every prompt about present-moment needs and helpful responses, never about what happened to bring on the flashback, since that detail is not required for either partner's part of this plan. The code word in the last prompt is often what partners use most, since it removes the pressure to explain anything in the moment itself.

title: Calm Places Passport Craft
summary: A decorated passport-style booklet of places and objects that help a child's body feel calm now.
goal: Use it to build a ready list of present-moment safe places instead of talking through what happened.
body_md: This stays entirely present-focused: a child draws or decorates calm places and comforting objects, never the event itself, so redirect gently back to the here-and-now if a child starts to narrate details. The caregiver's page turns the passport into a shared plan for actually revisiting these places together during the week. As with any safety-related work with a child, if a child discloses abuse or harm at any point, follow your mandated reporting duties right away.

goal: Use it to rehearse fast recognition of alarm signals and the grounding response that fits them.
body_md: Shuffle two piles, one of body-alarm cards and one of grounding-skill cards. Each turn, a player draws one card from each pile and argues whether it's a good match, and the group votes on whether the pairing works. Deliberate mismatches often generate the best discussion, so let a player defend an odd pairing before moving on. goal: Use it to separate lying-awake worry from the body's need to wind down before sleep.
duration: Five minutes nightly for two weeks
body_md: This is narrower than a full sleep hygiene review: it targets the specific moment anxiety shows up at bedtime and gives the client one alternative to problem-solving under the covers. Watch for clients using the log itself to keep planning or ruminating rather than noticing a pattern, and steer them back to the single wind-down step. Review the pattern line together after a week or two rather than each night.

goal: Use it to help clients notice the pull toward avoidance and pick one toward move instead.
body_md: Draw the choice point live with the client the first time, since sketching the fork between away moves and toward moves usually lands better than reading it off a sheet. Anxiety-specific away moves tend to be subtle, such as checking, seeking reassurance, or over-preparing, so help clients name the version they actually do rather than a generic one. The toward move at the end should be genuinely small enough to attempt this week.

goal: Use it to help clients state a need clearly instead of avoiding the ask altogether.
body_md: This applies the standard DEAR MAN sequence to a specific kind of moment: an ask the client keeps avoiding because anxiety predicts a bad reaction. Have the client script the words out loud in session before trying it for real, since anxious clients tend to soften the Assert line until it no longer functions as a request. goal: Use it to turn a child's coping steps into a memorable, personalized recipe they can reuse.
body_md: Have the child decorate the card like a real recipe, with a title, a short ingredients list, and simple steps, so the format feels playful rather than clinical. Keep ingredients concrete and physical, such as breathing, a hug, or a specific phrase, rather than abstract advice a child can't picture using. The caregiver's line turns this into something usable at home: a cue for catching early worry signs and prompting the recipe before worry builds.

goal: Use it to build quick recognition of early body signals and the skills that answer them.
body_md: Players take turns drawing a body-signal card, such as a racing heart or shaky hands, and act it out silently while the group guesses. goal: Use it to show clients exactly where one small change could interrupt their own cycle.

Most clients can name the withdrawal and the mood drop easily but miss the thought step in between, so slow down there. Set an explicit end date or check-in point so the arrangement stays time-limited rather than becoming a silent new normal. goal: Use it to surface which activities clients would actually choose versus what depression says to skip.

Players compete for the activities they actually want to try, which surfaces real preference faster than asking directly usually does. goal: Use it to build an off-ramp so hyperfocus does not quietly cancel the rest of a client's day.

goal: Use it to slow the gap between urge and action long enough for a thought to be examined.

The record works because it separates the thought from the action — many clients have never noticed there was a thought at all, only the outcome. One partner typically manages time and initiation more easily; the other may track details or follow through once a task is started. Naming those differences out loud, without judgment, is what lets the couple redesign who owns what instead of relitigating the same missed task every week.
