Partner A: tasks I consistently forget or put off
Partner B: tasks I start easily and follow through on
Partner B: tasks I consistently forget or put off
A task we will reassign based on what we just named
How we will remind each other without it turning into nagging
What we will say to each other when a task still gets missed

title: The Wiggle Break Wheel
summary: A spinner wheel of movement breaks that a child decorates and a caregiver uses between tasks.
goal: Use it to give a wiggly child a planned, physical outlet instead of a battle over sitting still.
body_md: Have the child draw, cut out, and color each wedge of movement — ten jumping jacks, an animal walk across the room, three spins in place — themselves, since ownership is what makes them use it later. The caregiver's job is to spin the wheel and hold the timer at agreed transition points, not to decide when a break is deserved, since that turns it back into a control fight. Keep wedges short enough that the break ends before it becomes the new distraction.

fields.label: Movement ideas I want on my wheel
Draw or decorate each wedge
When during the day my grown-up will spin it with me
How I will know when my break is over
What I do after the break is done

title: High-Risk Situation Rehearsal Card
summary: A card that walks a client through rehearsing a coping response before a known high-risk situation.
goal: Use it to have a coping response already rehearsed before urges arrive, not invented under pressure.
body_md: Build this for one specific situation the client has already identified as high-risk — a particular time, place, or person — rather than urges in general. Walk through the scene in detail and have the client say the coping line out loud, since rehearsal that stays silent in their head rarely holds up in the real moment. Revisit and rewrite the card after the situation actually happens, whether it went well or not.

fields.label: The specific situation I'm preparing for
What usually happens right before the urge shows up
The coping response I will use, in my own words
What I will do with my hands or body in that moment
Who I can contact if the urge is stronger than expected
What I will tell myself I already know how to do

title: Urge Defusion Card
summary: An ACT card that helps a client notice an urge as a passing thought rather than an instruction.
goal: Use it to create distance between noticing an urge and treating it as something that must be obeyed.
body_md: This is a brief defusion drill, not a distraction technique — the goal is for the client to notice the urge and the story attached to it, not to make the urge disappear. Have them practice saying “I'm having the urge that…” out loud before trying it silently during a real craving. Some clients want to argue with the urge instead of just naming it; gently redirect them back to noticing rather than debating.

fields.label: The urge as it actually showed up
The urge, named as a thought: I'm having the urge that...
What the urge is trying to convince me will happen if I don't act
What I actually value in this moment, urge aside
What I did instead of obeying the urge

title: Opposite Action for Urges
summary: A DBT worksheet that has a client identify the action an urge is pushing for, then deliberately do the opposite.
goal: Use it to practice acting against an urge's pull instead of following it automatically.
body_md: This only works when the client can name the urge accurately first, so slow down that step rather than rushing to the opposite action. Opposite action here is not white-knuckling; it's a specific, planned, different behavior done fully, not halfheartedly. Check in afterward on what happened in the body and mood once the opposite action was completed, since that follow-through is what teaches the nervous system something new.

fields.label: The urge and what it wants me to do
The situation that brought it on
The opposite action, stated as something concrete I can actually do
How I will do it fully, not halfway
What happened in my body and mood after

title: My Circle of Grown-Ups
summary: A drawing activity where a child maps the safe grown-ups they can go to when substance use affects their family.
goal: Use it to help a child name concrete safe adults and actions, separate from a family member's substance use.
body_md: The child draws themselves in the center and the safe grown-ups in their life around them, adding what each person can help with — a ride, a hug, a place to go. Keep language behavior-focused throughout, talking about someone's substance use and never a label for that person, and let the caregiver in session, if present, hear the child name what helps without correcting or defending. If the child discloses anything suggesting they are unsafe or unsupervised, pause the activity and follow your mandated reporting duties.

fields.label: Draw yourself in the middle of the circle
Draw or write the grown-ups who help keep you safe
What each person can help you with
A safe place I can go if things feel scary or confusing at home
One thing I want a grown-up to know about how I'm feeling

title: The Craving Clock Game
summary: A group game where players time how long an imagined urge lasts while using a coping skill, then compare notes.
goal: Use it to make the idea concrete that urges rise, peak, and pass if given time.
body_md: Each player draws a situation card describing a common trigger, picks a coping skill card, and the group sets a two-minute timer while that player narrates their imagined intensity out loud, high to low. The debrief is the point: compare how fast intensity dropped across different coping skills and situations, and let the group notice that no one's urge stayed at a ten for the full two minutes. Keep the tone playful, not testing, or players will perform certainty instead of reporting what they'd actually feel.

fields.label: Situation card drawn
Coping skill card drawn
Starting intensity, 1 to 10
Intensity at the end of the timer
What helped it drop, or what got in the way

title: Anger Aftermath Repair Plan
summary: A worksheet completed after an anger episode that plans the repair conversation and what to do differently.
goal: Use it to turn the period right after an outburst into a structured repair instead of avoidance.
body_md: Bring this in a session or two after an anger episode the client wants to repair, once they're regulated enough to look at it without reigniting. Separate the apology from the plan — clients often stop at sorry and skip naming what they'll actually do differently, which is what the other person usually needs to hear. If the episode involved a partner or family member, consider whether a joint session to deliver the repair together would land better than the client doing it alone.

fields.label: What happened, in a few neutral sentences
What I said or did that I want to repair
The impact on the other person, as best I can tell
What I will say when I approach them
What I will do differently if this situation comes up again
When I plan to have this conversation

title: Angry Passengers on the Bus
summary: An ACT exercise using the bus-driver metaphor to practice acting on values while anger rides along.
goal: Use it to help a client keep driving toward what matters without letting anger grab the wheel.
body_md: Introduce the metaphor first: the client is the driver, and anger, along with its usual demands to yell, slam, or shut down, is a loud passenger who doesn't actually hold the wheel. This works best paired with a real recent situation rather than staying abstract, so the client can picture the passenger's exact voice. Watch for clients who try to argue the passenger into silence; the aim is closer to acknowledging it's there and continuing to drive.

fields.label: A recent situation where angry passengers got loud
What that passenger was telling me to do
Where I actually wanted to drive, the value underneath
What I did instead of handing over the wheel
What I will say to that passenger next time it gets loud

title: Radical Acceptance for Old Anger
summary: A DBT worksheet applying radical acceptance to resentment a client has carried for a long time.
goal: Use it to loosen the grip of old anger that fighting reality has failed to resolve.
body_md: This is for the anger that's aged past the original event, when a client is still replaying something months or years old. Distinguish acceptance from approval early, since clients often hear this exercise as being asked to say the situation was fine; it wasn't, and the worksheet doesn't ask them to say it was. Expect resistance in the first pass; radical acceptance rarely lands as a single decision, and revisiting this worksheet across sessions is normal.

fields.label: The old situation I'm still carrying anger about
What I keep telling myself should have happened instead
What is actually true about it now, whether I like it or not
What fighting this reality has cost me so far
One sentence of acceptance I'm willing to try, even partly
What I want to do with my energy instead of replaying this

title: Partner Anger Trigger Exchange
summary: A couples worksheet where each partner names their own anger triggers before conflict, not during it.
goal: Use it to give both partners a map of what sets the other off, made in a calm moment.
body_md: Do this on a calm day, never mid-argument — the point is prevention, not a rulebook to weaponize later. Have each partner fill out their own column independently first, then trade and read the other's out loud, which often surfaces triggers the other partner never realized they were causing. Circle back to this worksheet after real disagreements to check whether a named trigger showed up and whether the requested response actually happened.

fields.label: Partner A: what tends to trigger my anger
Partner A: what helps me when I'm already angry
Partner A: what makes it worse
Partner B: what tends to trigger my anger
Partner B: what helps me when I'm already angry
Partner B: what makes it worse
One thing each of us will try differently based on what we just read

title: The Anger Scale Guessing Game
summary: A group game where players guess each other's anger rating for a scenario, then debrief the gaps.
goal: Use it to show how differently people rate the same situation on an anger scale.
body_md: One player reads a scenario card aloud, everyone privately writes a number from one to ten for how angry they'd feel, then all numbers are revealed at once. The gaps are the whole point: a scenario that lands as a two for one player and an eight for another opens a debrief about why, without anyone being told their number is wrong. Keep score loosely if at all — closeness to the group average is far less interesting than the reasons behind the spread.

fields.label: Scenario read aloud
My anger rating, 1 to 10
The group's range of ratings
What made my number different from someone else's
What I noticed about how people size up the same situation

title: OCD Theme Inventory
summary: A one-page map of which OCD themes show up most for this client right now.
goal: Use it to organize scattered obsessions and compulsions into named themes you can track together.
body_md: Many clients name one obsession when several run in parallel, and progress stalls when a theme goes untracked. Have the client list every theme they can identify before ranking them, since the ranking itself often reveals which one is actually driving the most distress. Revisit this sheet every few sessions, since themes shift as compulsions are given up and a new one sometimes moves in to take the vacated space.

fields.label: The themes my mind gets stuck on (checking, contamination, symmetry, harm, relationship, right or wrong, other)
For each theme, the obsession that runs through my head
For each theme, what I do to get rid of the obsession
Which theme takes up the most time right now
Which theme is the easiest one to start working on
What I notice in common across my themes

title: ERP Session Log
summary: A log for recording each exposure and response prevention practice and what happened.
goal: Use it to track discomfort ratings and ritual resistance across exposures so progress stays visible.
body_md: Clients tend to round their peak discomfort rating down once the exposure is over, so ask them to log it in the moment or as close to it as possible rather than from memory afterward. The most useful column is often the last one: a completed exposure with a partial ritual still counts as data, and naming exactly what happened teaches more than a pass or fail mark. Review the trend across entries together rather than judging any single exposure on its own.

fields.label: The exposure I practiced
My discomfort rating right before I started (0-10)
My discomfort rating at the peak
My discomfort rating at the end
Did I complete it without doing the compulsion? What happened instead
What I noticed about how the urge changed over time
What I want to try next time

title: TIPP for Compulsion Urges
summary: A card that applies the DBT TIPP skills to bring down a compulsion urge fast enough to sit with it.
goal: Use it when an urge to ritualize spikes and the client needs a few minutes of relief before choosing not to act on it.
body_md: TIPP was built to bring down emotional arousal fast, and a compulsion urge behaves the same way physiologically as any other spike in the DBT model. Use this in the middle of a hard moment rather than saving it for session: the point is to buy the client sixty to ninety seconds so the urge has room to fall before they decide whether to ritualize. It works better paired with a plan for what they will do with that window, since dropping the arousal without a next step often just delays the compulsion.

fields.label: The urge I'm having right now and how strong it feels (0-10)
Temperature: cold water on my face or hands, for 30 seconds
Intense exercise: a minute of jumping jacks or fast stair climbs
Paced breathing: longer exhale than inhale, for one minute
Paired muscle relaxation: tense and release, one minute
My urge rating now, and what I chose to do instead of the ritual

title: OCD Household Load Audit
summary: A worksheet mapping which household tasks have quietly shifted onto the partner without OCD.
goal: Use it to renegotiate a fairer division of labor without asking either partner to take over or drop compulsions.
body_md: Family accommodation logs usually track rituals directly; this one tracks the household labor that piles up around them, like grocery shopping handed over because of contamination fears, or nightly door checks the partner starts doing instead. Fill it out together rather than having the partner with OCD complete it alone, since the goal is a negotiated handback, not a confession. Move only one or two tasks at a time and expect the anxious partner's distress to spike before it settles, which is a sign the audit is working, not a reason to reverse the handback.

fields.label: Tasks that have shifted onto my partner because of checking, cleaning, or avoidance on my part
Tasks my partner has quietly taken over that I want back
What my partner needs from me before handing a task back
One task we will move back to me this month, and how
What my partner will do differently if I ask for reassurance instead of taking the task over
How we will each know the new split is working

title: Shrink the Ritual Chart
summary: A sticker chart that shrinks one compulsion down in small, plotted steps instead of stopping it all at once.
goal: Use it to give a child a visible, gradual path off one ritual without asking for a sudden full stop.
body_md: Build this with the child rather than handing it over finished, since choosing the first step themselves increases follow-through. Pick a ritual that is frequent but not the most distressing one to shrink first, so the early wins are believable. Coach the parent beforehand on responding to the smaller version with the same calm attention as the full ritual, since praising the shrink and getting anxious about the leftover piece undoes the point; the chart should track effort, not a clean finish line, and steps can stay the same size for more than one week if the child needs that.

fields.label: The check or ritual we are shrinking (draw or write it)
How I do it now (how many times, how long)
Step 1: a slightly smaller version I can try this week
A sticker or check mark for each day I do the smaller version
How the worry feeling changed after I tried it
Step 2: what a smaller version looks like next

title: Interoceptive Exposure Menu
summary: A menu of body-sensation exercises used to practice interoceptive exposure to panic sensations on purpose.
goal: Use it to build a graded list of sensation-inducing exercises so panic sensations lose their alarm value.
duration: 30 minutes to build, then repeated practice
body_md: Build the menu from sensations the client actively avoids noticing, not generic exercises, since a straw-breathing drill means nothing if their real trigger is a racing heart after caffeine. Each exercise should be repeated to the point of boredom in a single sitting rather than stopped at the first spike, because it is the repetition inside one practice that teaches the sensation is not dangerous. Rule out any exercise a medical provider has flagged as inappropriate before assigning it as homework.

fields.label: The sensation I'm most afraid of feeling (racing heart, dizziness, breathlessness, tight throat)
Exercise 1 and the sensation it brings on (example: spin in a chair, then dizziness)
My fear rating for this exercise before I try it (0-10)
What actually happened when I tried it, and for how long
My fear rating after several repeats
The next exercise, chosen because it brings on a sensation I still avoid
What I'm learning about what these sensations actually mean

title: Panic Choice Point Card
summary: An ACT Choice Point diagram applied to the moment right before a panic-driven exit or avoidance move.
goal: Use it to make the toward-and-away choice visible in the seconds before a client leaves or cancels out of panic.
body_md: Draw the choice point live in session before sending it home, since clients often cannot name their own away moves until they see one sketched out from a recent panic episode. The card works best kept somewhere they will see it right before entering a feared situation, not filed away with other worksheets. Expect the first few uses to end in the away move anyway; the goal at first is just noticing the choice point exists, not winning it every time.

fields.label: The situation where panic tends to show up
What panic is telling me to do (leave, cancel, avoid)
What that away move costs me, over time
What I actually care about being able to do here
A toward move I could make instead, even a small one
What I'll say to myself right at the choice point

title: Rebuilding Shared Outings Plan
summary: A plan for a couple to gradually reclaim outings and activities scaled back because of panic.
goal: Use it to rebuild a shared life around panic without either partner having to force a full return at once.
body_md: Couples often narrow their shared life gradually enough that neither partner notices how much has been dropped until this list is in front of them. The partner without panic usually wants to help by taking over logistics or staying unusually close, and this plan asks them to trade that role for something more useful: encouraging the smaller version and resisting the urge to rescue if things get uncomfortable. Choose activities either partner misses, not just the ones that look most impressive to fix first.

fields.label: Activities we used to do together that we've cut back or stopped
What I'm afraid will happen if we try one again
What my partner has been doing to help me avoid it (driving a certain way, staying close by, checking in constantly)
One activity we'll try again this month, in a smaller version
What my partner will do instead of the usual safety habit
How we'll each know the smaller version counts as a win

title: Big Wave Body Map
summary: A body outline a child colors to mark where panic sensations show up, paired with a calm-down step list.
goal: Use it to help a child name and locate sudden scary body feelings and pick calming steps in advance.
body_md: Some children experience panic without any language for it beyond 'I feel sick' or 'something bad is happening,' and mapping the sensations onto a body outline gives them words before asking them to use a coping skill. Do the coloring together in session first so the clinician can hear the child's own descriptions rather than supplying words for them. Coach the parent to use the same body-part language at home in the moment, asking whether this is a tummy wave or a heart wave, rather than asking the child to explain from scratch every time.

fields.label: Color the spots on my body where the big wave shows up (heart, tummy, throat, hands)
What each spot feels like (pounding, tight, shaky, hot)
What my body thinks is happening
What is really happening (my body's alarm going off, not real danger)
My first calm-down step
Who I can go to when the big wave hits

title: Panic Sensation Match
summary: A matching game pairing panic sensations with what is actually happening in the body, played in a group.
goal: Use it to replace catastrophic misreadings of body sensations with realistic ones through repeated matching.
body_md: Deal sensation cards, such as racing heart or tight chest, and explanation cards, such as adrenaline releasing or blood moving to the muscles, face down in two piles; players take turns flipping one of each and deciding whether they match, with the group correcting mismatches together. Keep one deliberately wrong explanation card in the deck to spark debate, since arguing over a bad match does more for belief change than a clean correct answer. Close with the debrief questions rather than moving straight on, since that's where sensations connect back to each player's own panic pattern.

fields.label: Sensation cards we used
Explanation cards we used
A match that surprised someone
A sensation someone still finds hard to believe is harmless
What we'll each do next time that sensation shows up

title: Behavior Priority Sort
summary: A worksheet sorting a child's behaviors into address now, watch, and let go, so a parent isn't fighting every battle.
goal: Use it to help a parent choose one or two target behaviors instead of reacting to everything at once.
body_md: Parents usually arrive with a much longer list than two behaviors, and this worksheet is where that list gets narrowed down rather than acted on directly. The let-go column tends to be the hardest to fill in and the most useful, since spreading attention across ten behaviors usually means none of them actually change. Revisit the sort every few weeks rather than adding new behaviors to an already full address-now column.

fields.label: Every behavior currently frustrating me, listed without editing
Which ones feel most urgent, and why
Behaviors I'll address now (no more than two)
Behaviors I'll watch but not react to yet
Behaviors I'm choosing to let go of for now, and what I'll say to myself when I want to react anyway
What consistent response I'll use for each address-now behavior

title: Willingness to Hold the Limit Practice
summary: An ACT willingness practice for staying present through a child's protest instead of giving in to end the discomfort.
goal: Use it to help a parent hold a boundary by making room for guilt and distress rather than avoiding them.
body_md: Most caving happens because a parent is trying to make their own discomfort go away, not because the limit was wrong, and this practice separates those two things. Have the client rehearse the willingness language out loud before the next likely protest, since it needs to be available in the moment, not just written down. This pairs well with a values conversation about the kind of parent they want to be, since willingness without a clear reason to hold the line rarely survives a real protest.

fields.label: The limit I keep caving on
What shows up in me right before I give in (guilt, their crying, my own anxiety)
What giving in actually costs, over time, for both of us
The kind of parent I want to be in this moment, even if it's uncomfortable
What I can say to myself while I make room for the discomfort and hold the limit anyway
What I noticed the last time I held it despite the urge to give in

title: Opposite Action for Parent Guilt Card
summary: A DBT opposite action card for when parent guilt urges giving in, apologizing excessively, or over-explaining a limit.
goal: Use it to help a parent check whether guilt fits the facts and act opposite to it when it doesn't.
body_md: Parent guilt is one of the more common places opposite action gets skipped in favor of just talking the guilt through, but the DBT move here is behavioral: check whether the guilt fits the facts, and if it doesn't, act the opposite of what it's pushing for instead of processing it further. Watch for the over-explaining pattern in particular, since a parent who re-justifies a fair limit to their child is usually acting on the guilt rather than the facts. This pairs well with a parent who has already tried thought-based guilt work and keeps caving anyway.

fields.label: The limit I set that triggered guilt
What the guilt is telling me to do (undo it, over-explain, apologize repeatedly)
Does the guilt fit the facts? Was the limit fair, safe, and reasonable for their age?
If the guilt doesn't fit, the opposite action I'll take instead
How I'll say the limit differently next time, without over-explaining
What happened when I acted opposite to the guilt

title: Teamwork Badge Craft
summary: A badge children design and earn for cooperating with a sibling, spotted and named by a coached parent.
goal: Use it to build sibling cooperation through immediate, specific parent praise rather than after-the-fact rewards.
body_md: Make the badge with the children rather than printing one, since a badge they designed themselves gets more mileage than a generic sticker chart. Coach the parent beforehand to name the specific cooperative behavior out loud the moment they see it, rather than waiting until the end of the day, since the timing does more work than the badge itself. Let children award a badge to a sibling occasionally too; that peer-to-peer praise often lands harder than anything from a parent.

fields.label: Design my teamwork badge (draw and color it)
What teamwork looks like that earns the badge (sharing, taking turns, helping)
A time this week I earned it
What my grown-up said when they noticed
Who I want to give a badge to next

title: Rules and Rewards Sorting Game
summary: A family card-sorting game matching behaviors to earned privileges or consequences to build one shared rule set.
goal: Use it to get everyone in the family sorting behaviors the same way before a real consequence is ever on the line.
body_md: Write behavior cards from real recent conflicts rather than generic examples, and shuffle in a couple of trick cards, like a chore done badly on purpose, to spark real disagreement. Each player takes a turn drawing a card and proposing where it goes, whether it earns a privilege, gets a consequence, or is a warning first, and the family has to reach agreement before it's placed. Run the debrief with the rule that whatever gets agreed on today gets used consistently this week, since the game only helps if it produces a rule that actually gets enforced afterward.

fields.label: Behavior cards we sorted
Where we disagreed on a card, and how we settled it
The final house rule for that behavior
A card that surprised someone once it was discussed
What we'll do differently now that we've agreed

title: Infant Feeding Stress and Support Plan
summary: A worksheet for naming feeding worries and lining up support before the next hard feed.
goal: Use it to turn free-floating stress about feeding choices into a concrete support plan.
body_md: Feeding decisions in the early weeks, whether breast, bottle, pumping, or some mix, tend to carry an outsized amount of judgment from strangers, family, and social media. Use this after a rough feed or a comment that stuck, not as a lactation consult substitute; route feeding logistics themselves to a lactation consultant or pediatrician and use this sheet for the emotional side. Watch for comparison to other parents doing it differently.

fields.label: What the feeding plan looked like before birth, and how it has actually gone
Comments or comparisons that have stuck with me
What I actually need right now around feeding
Who could help with this: partner, family, lactation support, pediatrician
One way I can ask for that help this week
A reminder to myself for the next hard feed

title: Sleep-Deprived Thinking Check
summary: A short thought record for catching catastrophic thinking that spikes with newborn sleep loss.
goal: Use it to slow down conclusions drawn in the middle of the night until rest returns.
body_md: Sleep deprivation reliably intensifies catastrophizing, mind reading, and black-and-white thinking in new parents, and thoughts that feel like facts at 3 a.m. often look different by mid-morning. Use this in the moment after a distressing thought rather than as a nightly homework habit, and keep it brief since attention and patience are both in short supply. Track hours of sleep alongside belief ratings so the pattern becomes visible over a few uses.

fields.label: The thought that showed up
How many hours of sleep I have had in the last 24
How much I believed the thought in the moment, 0 to 100
What a rested version of me might say back
One thing that would actually help right now
How much I believe the thought now

title: New Parent Help-Asking DEAR MAN
summary: A DEAR MAN script for asking a partner or relative for one concrete piece of baby help.
goal: Use it to turn a vague wish for help into a single, specific, askable request.
body_md: New parents often carry a wish for help that never gets voiced as an actual ask, partly from guilt and partly from not knowing what to request. Apply the standard DEAR MAN structure to one narrow, concrete ask, such as a single night feed or an hour of coverage, rather than a general plea for more support. Coach the client to pick the smallest workable request first so the skill has a good chance of landing, then build from there.

fields.label: Describe: what is actually happening right now, just the facts
Express: how this is affecting me
Assert: the one specific thing I am asking for
Reinforce: how it will help both of us if they say yes
Staying mindful: what I will do if they change the subject or say no at first
Appearing confident: how I want to sound saying this
Negotiate: something I could offer or adjust

title: New Parent Visitor Boundaries Agreement
summary: A joint planning sheet for agreeing on visitor limits before a newborn's first houseguests arrive.
goal: Use it to help both partners settle visitor rules before conflict erupts in the moment.
body_md: Partners often carry different family expectations about visiting a newborn, and exhaustion turns small disagreements about houseguests into flashpoints fast. Best used before the baby arrives or as early as possible after, this sheet has each partner name their own hopes and worries before negotiating shared rules, so neither person is blindsided later. Push for specifics on notice, length of visit, and what visitors can help with rather than vague good intentions.

fields.label: Partner A's honest hopes and worries about visitors
Partner B's honest hopes and worries about visitors
What we agree we both need in the first few weeks
Our shared rules: notice, length of visit, what visitors can help with
The one relative or situation we expect to be hardest
What Partner A will say if that boundary gets pushed
What Partner B will say if that boundary gets pushed
How we will check in with each other afterward

title: Fourth Trimester Trivia Challenge
summary: A trivia game where new parents guess what actually counts as normal after birth.
goal: Use it to normalize common fourth-trimester experiences and ease isolating comparison.
body_md: Read out a mix of statements about postpartum bodies, moods, sleep, and baby behavior, and have players vote true or false before you reveal the answer and award a point for each correct guess. This works especially well in new-parent groups, where hearing that a strange or hard experience is widely shared does more to ease isolation than reassurance alone. Keep statements general rather than citing specific numbers, and leave time to debrief on what felt most reassuring.

fields.label: Statements our group guessed correctly
Statements our group got wrong
The one 'normal' fact that surprised me most
Something happening for me that I now feel less alone in
A myth about new parenthood I want to let go of

title: Self-Worth Timeline Review
summary: A timeline mapping how a client's sense of self-worth has shifted across major life periods.
goal: Use it to locate when self-worth took a hit and what has protected it since.
body_md: Segment the client's life into rough chunks such as childhood, school years, early adulthood, and now, then rate self-worth in each period before looking for the events or relationships that shaped the drops and rises. This works well early in self-esteem-focused work to build a shared formulation, giving both of you a map rather than a single flat story. Watch for one especially hard stretch coming to define the whole line, and ask what was still true about the client even then.

fields.label: Life periods I will map, for example childhood, school years, early adulthood, now
My self-worth rating in each period, low to high
What was happening in the periods where it dropped
What was happening in the periods where it rose
A pattern I notice looking at the whole line
What I want the next stretch of the line to look like

title: Self-Worth Behavioral Experiment
summary: A behavioral experiment testing self-worth predictions against what actually happens.
goal: Use it to test beliefs like 'no one wants my opinion' against real evidence, not just a feeling.
body_md: Unlike a general behavioral experiment, this one is anchored specifically to a self-worth belief such as 'if I speak up I'll be seen as less than' or 'if I say no, I'll lose the relationship.' Have the client pick a small, low-stakes action that would test the belief, predict the outcome and rate their belief before acting, then record what actually happened afterward. Running several small experiments across different situations builds an evidence base that outweighs any single bad memory.

fields.label: The self-worth belief I am testing
How much I believe it right now, 0 to 100
The small action I will take to test it
What I predict will happen
What actually happened
How much I believe the original belief now
What this experiment adds to my evidence

title: Scorecard Mind Defusion
summary: A defusion exercise for the part of the mind that constantly scores and ranks self-worth.
goal: Use it to notice the scorekeeping voice without automatically treating its verdicts as fact.
body_md: Introduce the metaphor of a 'scorecard mind' that keeps a running tally, adding and subtracting points for looks, achievement, or mistakes, and comparing the total to everyone else's. Have the client describe how their own scorecard talks, notice where it shows up in the body, and practice a short defusion phrase such as 'there's the scorecard again' to create some distance from it. The aim is not to silence the voice or win an argument with it, but to keep acting on values even while it is running.

fields.label: What my scorecard mind tends to keep tabs on
A recent score it handed me, and what triggered it
What I notice in my body when it is adding up points
A phrase I can use to notice it out loud
Something I would do today if the score did not get a vote

title: Partner Evidence Exchange for Self-Worth
summary: A structured exchange where each partner offers specific evidence for the other's worth.
goal: Use it to build an external evidence bank a partner with low self-worth can draw on later.
body_md: Have each partner separately write several specific, concrete examples of times the other showed competence, kindness, or worth, rather than general compliments, then take turns reading them aloud. The listening partner records which examples land hardest and keeps a couple to reread later. This supplements rather than replaces the client's own internal evidence-building work, so watch for a partner who slides into blanket reassurance instead of naming specifics.

fields.label: Partner A's specific examples of Partner B's worth, not general compliments
Partner B's specific examples of Partner A's worth, not general compliments
Which example landed hardest for Partner A, and why
Which example landed hardest for Partner B, and why
One example each of us will keep and reread this week

title: I Am Statements Mirror Frame
summary: A decorated mirror frame craft that displays a child's own positive 'I am' statements.
goal: Use it to give a child daily visual reminders of strengths they picked for themselves.
body_md: The child decorates a cardboard frame, or borders a real mirror with removable stickers, then writes or dictates several 'I am' statements such as brave, kind, or a good helper around the edge. A parent or caregiver mounts it by the child's mirror at home and is asked to read it aloud together at a set moment, like before school. Watch for children reaching for statements that please the adults in the room, and gently redirect toward specific things the child has actually done.

fields.label: Words or pictures I want on my frame
My 'I am' statements
Where at home this will go
Who will read it with me, and when

title: Visible Anxiety Symptom Belief Test
summary: A behavioral experiment testing beliefs about how visible anxiety symptoms are to others.
goal: Use it to compare predicted visibility of blushing or shaking with what others actually notice.
body_md: Many clients with social anxiety believe blushing, shaking, or sweating are far more obvious than they really are. Before a feared situation, have the client rate how visible they predict a symptom will be, then afterward compare that with actual evidence, whether from a trusted person's honest report or their own observation of others' reactions. Safety behaviors such as covering the face or avoiding eye contact will contaminate the result, so agree in advance to drop them for this test.

fields.label: The situation and the physical symptom I am worried will show
How visible I predict it will be to others, 0 to 100
How anxious that prediction makes me, 0 to 100
What actually happened, and any evidence I gathered
How visible it actually seemed to others, 0 to 100
What I am taking from the gap between prediction and reality

title: Critic in the Crowd Defusion
summary: A defusion practice for the felt sense that everyone in a room is silently judging.
goal: Use it to create distance from the 'critic in the crowd' story without arguing it away.
body_md: In social situations the mind often narrates a 'critic in the crowd' who is watching and judging every move, even when no one nearby is paying that much attention. Ask the client to describe this critic's voice and favorite lines, notice where it shows up in the body, and rehearse a short defusion phrase such as 'there's the critic again' to use before and during a mildly feared social moment. This pairs well with exposure work and a values-based reason for showing up anyway, rather than replacing either.

fields.label: What the critic in the crowd usually says
Where I feel it show up in my body
A situation where the critic gets loudest
My defusion phrase for noticing it
What I would do in that situation if the critic did not get a vote

title: Pre-Event TIPP Reset
summary: A TIPP-based routine for calming physical arousal in the minutes before a feared social event.
goal: Use it to bring arousal down before overwhelm can shape a decision to avoid.
body_md: Adapt the DBT TIPP skill, temperature, intense exercise, paced breathing, and paired muscle relaxation, to the narrow window right before something like a party, meeting, or date. Help the client pick which pieces are realistic to do in a car, a bathroom, or a hallway on the way in, since not every option fits every setting. Check temperature options such as cold water on the face against any relevant medical conditions, and keep intense exercise brief and appropriate to the client's fitness.

fields.label: The event I am using this before
My arousal level right before starting, 0 to 100
Which TIPP option I will use here
Where and how I will actually do it
My arousal level right after
What I will do next, however I am feeling

title: Meeting Someone New Puppet Script
summary: A puppet-and-script craft where a child builds and rehearses lines for meeting a new peer.
goal: Use it to rehearse a simple greeting script until it feels less unfamiliar out loud.
body_md: Have the child make a simple puppet from a paper bag, sock, or cutout, then write a short script together for meeting someone new: a name, one question, and one line for if the other kid says something unexpected. Practice with the puppet doing the talking first, then have the child speak the same lines as themselves. Ask the caregiver to run through the script once at home before the next real chance to use it, keeping the tone playful rather than like a test to pass.

fields.label: My puppet's name
What I will say first when I meet someone new
One question I can ask them
What I will say if they say something I do not expect
Who I practiced this with at home

title: Eye Contact Challenge Game
summary: A paired game that builds tolerance for eye contact through short, escalating rounds.
goal: Use it to make eye contact feel like a game with rules, not a test to fail.
body_md: Pair players up and hold eye contact for a set number of seconds each round, starting around three and building up, then break and rate discomfort before rotating partners in a group setting. Add a silly variant where the first person to laugh restarts the round, which keeps the exercise light rather than tense. Debrief afterward on how discomfort shifted from the first round to the last, and where else eye contact tends to get avoided day to day. Let anyone skip a round without needing to explain why.

fields.label: Starting discomfort rating before round one, 0 to 100
How long we held eye contact each round
Discomfort rating after the last round
What changed between round one and the last round
One place outside this room where I avoid eye contact

title: Ambiguous Loss Inventory
summary: Helps a client name and validate a loss that others may not recognize as grief-worthy.
goal: Use it to validate grief that friends and family have dismissed or overlooked.
body_md: Ambiguous loss covers grief that lacks a funeral or a clear ending — a friendship that faded, an estrangement, a miscarriage, a health condition that changed who someone was while they were still alive. Clients often arrive apologizing for grieving "something that doesn't count." Normalize the loss before moving through the prompts, and expect some clients to surface more sadness or anger than they anticipated once it is named directly.

fields.label: What did I lose, even though no one else may call it a loss?
What has made it hard for others to recognize this loss?
What have I told myself I'm not allowed to feel about it?
Who, if anyone, has acknowledged this loss with me?
What would I want someone to say to me about it?
One way I can honor this loss on my own terms

title: Grief Coping Workability Sort
summary: A card sort that checks whether a grief coping habit moves a client toward or away from their values.
goal: Use it to replace judgment about coping choices with a workability lens.
body_md: Write a list of grief-related coping behaviors — avoiding photos, staying busy, drinking more, isolating, visiting the grave weekly, talking about the person often — on cards ahead of time, or build the list with the client first. Sort each into workable or costly, then discuss the ones that land in both piles, since most do. The goal isn't to eliminate coping behaviors but to notice which ones the client wants to keep on purpose versus which ones have quietly taken over.

fields.label: A coping behavior I sorted into 'moves me toward my values'
A coping behavior I sorted into 'moves me away from my values'
A behavior that landed in both piles, and why
One coping behavior I want to keep on purpose
One coping behavior I want to loosen my grip on

title: Grief Burst Distress Skills Card
summary: A pocket card matching sudden waves of grief to a quick distress tolerance skill.
goal: Use it to give clients a fast, rehearsed response when a grief burst hits without warning.
body_md: Grief bursts arrive without much warning — a song, a smell, an empty chair at dinner — and clients often feel ambushed by their own reaction in public or at work. Build the card together in session by matching a few known triggers to a specific, already-rehearsed skill such as paced breathing, a cold-water reset, stepping outside, or texting a support person, rather than leaving the response to be improvised in the moment. Revisit and edit the card as new triggers show up.

fields.label: A trigger that tends to set off a grief burst for me
The first thing I will do in the first 60 seconds
A skill I can use if I'm in public and can't step away
Who I can text or call afterward
What I will tell myself while the wave passes

title: Reconnecting After Loss Conversation
summary: A guided conversation for partners to check in on the closeness a shared loss has disrupted.
goal: Use it to help a grieving couple rebuild connection without pressuring either partner's pace.
body_md: Grief can pull partners apart even when the loss is shared — one partner may want closeness while the other withdraws, or both quietly stop reaching for each other. Run this in session first so each partner can hear the other's answers without feeling ambushed at home, and watch for one partner using the loss as a reason to avoid an older disconnect that predates it. This is about noticing distance and naming small steps back, not about resolving the grief itself.

fields.label: Since the loss, what I miss most about how we used to connect
A moment recently when I felt closer to my partner
A moment recently when I felt more distant
One small thing my partner could do that would help me feel less alone
One small thing I am willing to try this week

title: Grief Myths and Facts Showdown
summary: A card game where players guess whether a statement about grief is a myth or a fact.
goal: Use it to correct unhelpful beliefs about grief timelines, stages, and moving on.
body_md: Prepare a deck of statements such as "grief moves through five stages in order" or "you should be over it after a year" mixed with accurate statements, then have players guess myth or fact before you reveal the answer and discuss. The debrief matters more than the score — pause on any myth a player believed personally, since these are often the exact beliefs driving guilt about grieving "wrong" or too long.

fields.label: A myth I used to believe about grief
A fact that surprised me
A belief about grief I inherited from my family
What I would tell someone else about how grief actually works

title: Relationship Pattern Timeline
summary: A worksheet mapping the relationship dynamic a client keeps repeating across different partners.
goal: Use it to help a client see a pattern clearly before deciding whether to repeat or change it.
body_md: This is individual work, done without a partner in the room, looking across two or three past or present relationships for a repeating role, dynamic, or turning point. Clients sometimes resist at first, worried this will turn into blaming themselves for everything that went wrong; frame it as pattern-spotting rather than fault-finding. The most useful moment is usually the last prompt, where the client names what they'd want to do differently now that the pattern is visible.

fields.label: Relationship one: what role did I tend to play?
Relationship two: what role did I tend to play?
What tends to happen around the point things start to break down?
What do these relationships have in common?
What part of the pattern is mine to change?
What do I want to do differently going forward?

title: Relationship Catastrophizing Thought Record
summary: A thought record for catching all-or-nothing predictions about a relationship's future during conflict.
goal: Use it to slow down thoughts like this always happens before they drive a bigger reaction.
body_md: Best used shortly after a disagreement, while the memory is fresh but the client is no longer flooded. Watch for the classic relationship catastrophizing moves — "we always fight about this," "this proves we're incompatible," "it's never going to change" — and help the client separate the specific incident from the sweeping verdict attached to it. This works well paired with a calmer follow-up conversation once the thought has been challenged rather than acted on.

fields.label: What happened, in a few neutral sentences
The catastrophic thought that showed up
How much I believed it in the moment, 0 to 100
Evidence that doesn't fit this thought
A more balanced way to think about this one incident
How much I believe the catastrophic thought now, 0 to 100

title: Wise Mind Pause Before the Hard Talk
summary: A short check-in that helps a client find wise mind before raising a sensitive relationship topic.
goal: Use it to replace impulsive blow-ups or silent avoidance with a chosen, wise-mind approach.
body_md: This is meant to be used in the five minutes before a client raises something difficult with a partner, not analyzed after the fact. Have them rate whether they're closer to emotion mind or reasonable mind, name the urge each is pulling toward such as attacking or saying nothing at all, and choose one wise-mind opening line before they start the conversation. Clients who tend to avoid entirely and clients who tend to escalate get different value from this, so tailor the debrief to which pattern shows up.

fields.label: What I want to raise with my partner
Where I am right now: emotion mind, reasonable mind, or between
What emotion mind wants me to do
What reasonable mind wants me to do
My wise-mind opening line

title: Life Transition Role Renegotiation
summary: A worksheet for a couple to renegotiate who does what after a major life transition shifts old roles.
goal: Use it after a job change, move, retirement, or illness to update expectations instead of assuming.
body_md: Roles that worked before a transition — who managed money, who ran the household, who worked outside the home — often stay on autopilot after the transition has already changed the reality on the ground, and resentment builds quietly on both sides. Have each partner complete their columns separately first, then compare in session, and expect at least one role neither partner realizes has gone unclaimed since the change. Revisit this again a few months after the transition, not just once.

fields.label: What changed for us, the transition itself
A role I used to have that no longer fits
A role my partner used to have that no longer fits
What I need from my partner now that wasn't true before
One role we will explicitly reassign this week

title: Sibling Peace Treaty Craft
summary: Siblings decorate and sign a written agreement listing the ground rules that ended their last fight.
goal: Use it to turn a repeated sibling conflict into a shared, visible agreement both children helped write.
body_md: Do this once things have cooled down, never mid-conflict, and let both children propose rules before you shape the wording, since a treaty they help write gets followed far more than one handed to them. The caregiver's job afterward is to post the treaty somewhere visible, reference it calmly by name during the next flare-up such as asking what the treaty says, and praise both children when they follow it rather than only stepping in when they don't.

fields.label: What we were fighting about
One rule I promise to follow
One rule my sibling promised to follow
What we will do instead of fighting next time
A picture or decoration for our treaty

title: Trust Generalization Check
summary: A thought record testing whether a no one is safe belief fits the trustworthy people in a client's life now.
goal: Use it to separate a specific past harm from a blanket rule applied to everyone in the present.
body_md: Keep this entirely in the present tense — the prompts ask about current relationships and current evidence, not what happened before, and should never be used to draw out details of past abuse. Clients with this history often carry an efficient but costly rule that protected them once and now isolates them; the aim is not to argue them out of caution but to test the rule against specific people already in their life. Go slowly if the client becomes activated, and return to grounding before ending the session.

fields.label: The rule I carry about who can be trusted
A person in my life now who this rule may not fit
Evidence for why this person might be safe to trust a little
Evidence that makes me cautious, even now
One small, low-risk way to test trust with this person
What I will do to ground myself if this feels like too much

title: Trust Rebuilding Values Ladder
summary: A step-by-step ladder that paces trust and connection toward what a client actually values.
goal: Use it to build committed action toward closeness at a pace the client's fear can tolerate.
body_md: This stays entirely forward-facing: the client identifies what connection or closeness they want more of now, then builds a ladder of small, willingness-based steps toward it, from lowest to highest fear. It is not an exposure hierarchy aimed at abuse memories and should never ask the client to revisit what happened. Expect the bottom rungs to look smaller than clients think they should need, which is normal, and rushing the ladder tends to backfire more than moving slowly does.

fields.label: What I want more of in my relationships, the value underneath this
A very small step toward that, one I could do this week
A medium step, further out
A bigger step I'm working toward, not yet
What fear tends to show up, and what I'll do to make room for it

title: Safe Closeness Menu for Partners
summary: A menu both partners build together of non-sexual affection that currently feels safe and welcome.
goal: Use it to give a couple a concrete, agreed starting point when a history of sexual abuse affects pacing.
body_md: This addresses how one partner's history shapes intimacy and pacing for the couple, not the history itself, and nothing here should ask either partner to describe what happened. Have each partner list forms of closeness such as hand-holding, sitting back-to-back, a hug at the door, or a check-in text that they currently welcome, are unsure about, or want to hold off on, then compare lists together. Revisit the menu regularly, since what belongs in each column can shift, and remind both partners that either can move something to a different column at any time without needing to explain why.

fields.label: A form of closeness that feels good and welcome right now
A form of closeness I'm unsure about
A form of closeness I want to hold off on for now
How I'd like my partner to check in before initiating
What support I need from my partner if I need to pause

title: Safety Voice Puppet Practice
summary: Children build a simple puppet and use it to rehearse saying no and telling a safe adult.
goal: Use it to give a child a rehearsed, playful way to practice body safety rules and telling a trusted adult.
body_md: Keep this squarely at the level of general body safety rules and rehearsal, such as practicing a firm no, a loud stop, and telling a safe adult right away, and never use it to ask a child to describe a specific event. The caregiver decorates a puppet alongside the child and takes a turn practicing the same lines, which makes the rehearsal feel like play rather than a test. If a child discloses anything during this activity, stop the exercise and follow your mandated reporting duties right away; this tool is for rehearsal and prevention, not for gathering disclosure details.

fields.label: My puppet's name
What my puppet says if a touch feels not okay
Who my puppet's safe grown-ups are
What my puppet does if something feels wrong
A time I want to practice with my puppet again

title: Trusted Grown-Up Relay Game
summary: A relay race where children answer body safety and trusted-adult questions before tagging their teammate.
goal: Use it to rehearse body safety rules and naming safe adults in a fast-paced, playful format.
body_md: Set up two short relay lines with a stack of simple scenario cards at the far end covering okay or not-okay touch, who counts as a safe adult, and what to say and do, then have each player run down, answer one card correctly with a helping adult's support if needed, and tag the next teammate. Keep every card at the level of general rules, never a specific event, and end with a group debrief naming each child's own safe adults out loud. Watch for any child who seems distressed rather than playful and pull them aside gently rather than continuing the game.

fields.label: A safety rule I answered correctly
One of my own safe grown-ups
Something I want to remember from today's game
A question I still have about staying safe

title: Coping Skills Sorted by Feeling State
summary: A sheet that sorts a client's coping skills by the internal state they answer, not the situation.
goal: Use it to help a client reach for a skill that matches how their body and mind feel right now.
body_md: Clients often have a long list of coping skills but freeze on which one to use, because most lists are organized by situation rather than by internal state. This sheet sorts skills into four columns: numb or shut down, wired or keyed up, spiraling thoughts, and lonely or low. Build the columns together from skills the client has already tried, and press for at least two entries per column before moving on. Revisit it after a hard week and move entries between columns as you learn what actually helps in each state.

fields.label: Skills that help when I feel numb or shut down
Skills that help when I feel wired or keyed up
Skills that help when my thoughts are spiraling
Skills that help when I feel lonely or low
How I can tell which state I am in before I pick a skill
A skill I want to try adding to one of these columns

title: Coping Skills in Service of Values
summary: Links each coping skill a client uses to the value it clears space to act on afterward.
goal: Use it to keep coping skills in service of a valued life rather than an end in themselves.
body_md: This is a defusion move for clients who have plenty of coping skills but use them to disappear from life rather than to re-enter it. For each skill, the client names not just that it lowered distress but what it then let them do that mattered to them, however small. If a client cannot name anything a skill made possible, flag it in session; that is often a sign the skill has become an avoidance strategy rather than a bridge back to a value. Keep the tone curious rather than corrective when that shows up.

fields.label: A coping skill I use often
What it does for me in the moment
What it lets me do afterward that matters to me
A time the skill helped me get back to something I value
A time I used the skill just to disappear, with nothing after it
One value I want a skill to point back toward this week

title: Skill Stack Sequence Card
summary: A card that orders three DBT skills into a first, backup, and fallback sequence for rising distress.
goal: Use it to give a client a rehearsed order of skills rather than a flat list to choose from under pressure.
body_md: Diary cards and skills lists tell a client what is available, but under real distress people rarely scan a full list and pick well. This card has them commit in advance to a first skill (often a body-based one like paced breathing or a TIPP technique), a backup if the first does not land within a few minutes, and a fallback for when distress is still climbing, usually a distraction or self-soothe skill. Rehearse the sequence out loud in session, including what tells the client it is time to move to the next step, and troubleshoot access issues for each one before they leave.

fields.label: My first skill to try
How I will know it is time to move to my backup
My backup skill
My fallback skill if distress is still climbing
What could get in the way of using this sequence
How this sequence worked the last time I used it

title: Coping Skills Suitcase Craft
summary: A child packs a paper suitcase with drawings of coping skills for an upcoming hard moment.
goal: Use it to help a child prepare concrete, portable coping tools before a specific stressful event.
body_md: Cut a large suitcase shape from card stock with a flap that opens, and have the child draw or cut out small pictures of coping skills to pack inside, framed around one upcoming trip they are nervous about, such as a doctor visit, a first day, or a sleepover. Keep the packing concrete: a picture of a stuffed animal for the self-soothing item, a breathing cloud, a photo of a trusted adult. The caregiver's job afterward is to actually bring the suitcase along or recreate its contents on the day, and to name out loud which packed skill they are using in the moment so the child sees it modeled.

fields.label: What hard moment am I packing for?
A coping skill I am packing (draw or write it)
Another coping skill I am packing
One more thing I am packing
Who will help me carry my suitcase on the day
For the grown-up: how we will use the suitcase on the day

title: Coping Skills Showdown
summary: A bracket-style elimination game where coping skill cards face off and the group votes a round winner.
goal: Use it to generate lively debate about what makes a coping skill fit a given moment.
body_md: Write eight to sixteen coping skills on cards and set them up in a single-elimination bracket. For each matchup, read a short scenario card and have the group vote which of the two paired skills fits it better; the winner advances. The fun is in the arguing, so let players make a case for an underdog skill before the vote. End with the two finalists facing off on a genuinely hard scenario, then debrief on how the same skill lost in one round and won in another, which is the real point: fit depends on context, not on any skill being universally best.

fields.label: Skills we put in our bracket
A matchup that sparked the most debate
Our final two skills and the scenario they faced
What we noticed about the same skill winning in one round and losing in another
A skill that lost every round for me but I still want to keep

title: Fear Origin Timeline
summary: Traces when and how a specific fear first took hold and what has kept it going.
goal: Use it to build a shared history of the fear before starting hierarchy or exposure work.
body_md: Before building a hierarchy, it helps to know whether a fear arrived through a frightening direct experience, watching someone else react fearfully, being told repeatedly that something was dangerous, or no clear event at all. None of these origins change the plan much, but naming one often reduces the confusion and self-blame clients feel about a fear that seems to have appeared from nowhere. Watch for clients who reach for a dramatic origin story that does not quite fit; a vague or absent memory is common and is fine to leave as such.

fields.label: The earliest memory I have connected to this fear
Was there a specific frightening event, or has it always been there?
Did anyone close to me react fearfully to this same thing?
What I was told about this thing growing up
How the fear has changed in size or reach since it started
What, if anything, has kept the fear going

title: Fear Generalization Map
summary: Maps how a fear has spread outward from its original object to related situations over time.
goal: Use it to find where a fear has generalized so exposure work targets the right layers.
body_md: Specific fears rarely stay contained; a fear of one dog can spread to all dogs, then to the sound of barking, then to walks where a dog might appear. This map starts with the original feared object at the center and has the client add rings outward for each related situation the fear has spread to, in the order it happened if they can recall it. The map often reveals that the outer rings are more avoidable and more impairing day to day than the original trigger, which can shift where exposure work starts.

fields.label: The original feared object or situation
The first related situation the fear spread to
Situations further removed that now trigger fear too
Which ring causes the most disruption to my daily life
A situation I avoid completely because of this spread
Where I want to start working first, and why

title: Stay-in-It Countdown Card
summary: Pairs a fixed countdown with a distress tolerance skill so a client stays in a feared moment rather than escaping.
goal: Use it to give a client a concrete, timed alternative to escaping a feared situation early.
body_md: Escaping a feared situation the moment distress spikes is what keeps a phobia intact, but telling a client to simply tolerate the feeling rarely works on its own. This card sets a specific count, such as sixty seconds or ten breaths, paired with one distress tolerance skill the client will run during that count, then has them log where their fear actually peaked and where it landed by the end of the count. Most clients are surprised the peak arrives sooner than they expect. Use short counts at first and lengthen them only as the client's confidence in the pairing grows.

fields.label: The situation I am staying in
My countdown length
The distress tolerance skill I am running during the count
Fear level at the start of the count (0 to 10)
Fear level at the end of the count (0 to 10)
What I noticed about where the fear peaked

title: Phobia Accommodation Reduction Plan
summary: Helps a couple name the accommodations one partner makes for the other's fear and plan to reduce them gradually.
goal: Use it to shrink the accommodations that unintentionally keep a partner's fear in place.
body_md: When one partner has a specific fear, the other often quietly takes over related tasks entirely, from handling anything that flies to always driving on the highway, which eases short-term distress but keeps the fear intact and can breed quiet resentment on both sides. This plan has the fearful partner name each accommodation and rate how much it helps versus how much it reinforces avoidance, while the accommodating partner names what that accommodating actually costs them. Agree together on one accommodation to reduce first, and what support looks like as the task shifts back.

fields.label: Partner with the fear: tasks my partner currently handles because of my fear
Partner with the fear: which of these I could start taking back on, with support
Accommodating partner: what taking on these tasks costs me
Accommodating partner: what support I can offer as my partner takes a task back
The one accommodation we are agreeing to reduce first
How we will check in with each other as this changes

title: Whose Fear Is It Anyway
summary: A guessing game where anonymous fears are read aloud and the group guesses who wrote each one.
goal: Use it to normalize specific fears and lower shame before hierarchy work begins.
body_md: Each player writes one specific fear on an unsigned card and drops it in a container. Shuffle and read the fears aloud one at a time, letting the group guess who wrote each before the writer reveals themselves. The reveals usually surprise people, since confident-seeming group members often turn out to have the most vivid fears, and that mismatch does most of the normalizing work. Close by having each player pick one fear from the pile, their own or someone else's, and name where it might sit on a hierarchy from mild to severe.

fields.label: The fear I wrote on my card
A fear someone else shared that surprised me
How it felt to have my fear guessed, or guessed wrong
What I noticed about how common specific fears turned out to be
Where my own fear might sit on a hierarchy from mild to severe

title: Body Image Trigger Map
summary: Maps the specific situations, people, and settings that spike appearance-focused distress.
goal: Use it to identify concrete triggers rather than leaving body image distress as a vague, constant backdrop.
body_md: Clients often describe body image distress as constant, but it usually spikes around specific, nameable triggers: certain lighting, particular clothing, specific people's comments, or particular apps at particular times of day. This map has the client list triggers across a few categories and rate the intensity each brings up, which turns an overwhelming, undifferentiated feeling into something with edges the client can plan around. Use the map to choose one or two triggers to work with directly rather than trying to address everything at once.

fields.label: Places or settings that spike appearance-focused distress
People or comments that spike it
Specific times of day or situations that spike it
Apps, sites, or media that spike it
Which trigger feels most intense, rated 0 to 10
One trigger I want to work on first

title: Appearance Rule Cost-Benefit Ledger
summary: Weighs what a client's strict appearance-related rule actually gives them against what it costs.
goal: Use it to loosen the grip of a specific appearance rule by making its real costs visible.
body_md: Clients with body image concerns often live by unspoken rules, such as never leaving the house without makeup or always wearing certain clothing to hide a feature they dislike. This ledger picks one such rule and lays out what the client believes it protects them from against what it actually costs in time, spontaneity, and mental energy. The point is not to argue the client out of the rule in one sitting, but to make the trade explicit enough that a small, time-limited experiment with bending it becomes thinkable.

What I believe would happen if I broke this rule
What this rule gives me or protects me from
What this rule costs me in time, energy, or freedom
A small, time-limited way I could bend this rule
What I noticed after trying it

title: Appearance Story Defusion Card
summary: Practices holding an appearance-critical thought as a passing story rather than a fact to act on.
goal: Use it to build distance from appearance-critical thoughts without arguing them into being false.
body_md: Rather than disputing an appearance-critical thought as true or false, this card has the client notice it and relabel it as a story their mind is telling, using the standard defusion frame of "I'm noticing my mind is telling me the story that...". Practice this in session first with a mild example before the client tries it on a stronger one; the wording feels awkward at first and clients often want to skip straight to arguing the content instead. The goal is distance from the thought, not agreement or disagreement with it.

The same thought reframed as: I'm noticing my mind is telling me the story that...
How it felt to hold the thought this way instead of arguing with it
A moment this week I could try this with a new thought
What I did instead of acting on the thought

title: Shared Media Feed Audit
summary: Has both partners review what appearance-focused content they follow and agree on changes together.
goal: Use it to turn media habits that fuel comparison into something a couple manages together.
body_md: Appearance-focused comparison is often fed by media one partner scrolls alone, and the other partner may not know which accounts or content are hardest on their partner's self-perception. This audit has each partner separately list a few accounts or types of content that leave them feeling worse about their appearance, then share the lists with each other. From there they agree on one concrete change each, such as muting an account or adding a different kind of content, and one way the other partner can check in without it turning into surveillance.

Partner B: content or accounts that leave me feeling worse about how I look
What surprised each of us about the other's list
One change each partner is making to their own feed
How we will check in on this without it feeling like monitoring

title: Kind Mirror Frame Craft
summary: A child decorates a frame to keep near a mirror at home, filled with kind things to say to themselves.
goal: Use it to build a habit of kind self-talk in the exact moment appearance-focused thoughts tend to show up.
body_md: Give the child a plain cardboard or paper frame, small enough to lean near a mirror at home, and have them decorate it and write or draw a few kind phrases inside, things they can say to themselves rather than comments about how they look. The caregiver's job is to place the frame near a mirror the child uses daily and say one of the phrases aloud themselves sometimes, modeling that grown-ups need reminders too. If the child leans toward harsh self-comments already, redirect gently toward phrases about how they treat others or what they enjoy doing.
